documentation.range: The Komodo Dragon occurs in eight discrete subpopulations: three on Flores (including the outlying Longos and Ontoloe Islands); and five on islands within Komodo National Park: Komodo, Rinca, Padar (from which it was lost in the late 1970s but a small subpopulation now exists following recolonization in 2004 and at least one subsequent deliberate translocation), Nusa Kode and Gili Motang (Jessop et al. in prep.). The area of suitable habitat which is actually occupied by this species has been estimated at around 809 km2, based on a combination of systematic direct animal trapping and camera trap observations at around 550 localities throughout the range between 2002 and 2019 (Jessop et al. in prep.). This small area of occupancy relative to the size of the species' range (with only 509 km2 of suitable habitat found on Flores, the largest island within its range with an area of 16,000 km2) is thought to reflect a combination of abiotic factors, the species' ecological preferences, and the impacts of anthropogenic habitat loss and degradation on Flores (Jessop et al. in prep.). There appears to have been a slow decline in the species' area of occupancy based on comparison with surveys conducted by Auffenberg (1969–1970), estimated at around 12% over a three-generation (45 year) period and driven entirely by a reduction in occupancy on Flores (principally in the island's northwest), with no evidence of any change in occupancy on Komodo (Jessop et al. in prep.).
documentation.population:
The global population is estimated to consist of 1,383 mature individuals (and an estimated 3,458 individuals including juveniles but not arboreal hatchlings), with about 68% of the population on Komodo and Rinca together (Jessop et al. in prep.). Rinca appears to hold the largest subpopulation, in the range of 1,119–1,493 animals (estimated 474 adults), with comparable but slightly lower numbers on Komodo. These authors estimate around 10% of viable hatchlings survive to maturity. These authors summarize population estimates for each subpopulation, at least two of which - on Padar and North West Flores - contain only three mature individuals and fewer than 10 in total (Jessop et al. in prep.). Both the Gili Motang and Nusa Kode subpopulations are estimated to consist of fewer than 100 individuals including juveniles (Jessop et al. in prep.). The methodology used to derive these estimates differ by island: the Komodo population was subject to long-term mark-recapture monitoring, while the Flores data were obtained using "low-density camera trapping" during the occupancy study (Jessop et al. in prep.).

Across the population as a whole, there are an estimated 415 mature females (Jessop et al. in prep.). Most females breed annually but some are biennial,  based on five years of nesting surveys, suggesting that the breeding population is about 0.8 of the total number of adult females (i.e. 332) (Jessop et al. in prep.).

The population trend was estimated from 11 sites within Komodo National Park and seven on Flores  using "accepted quantitative methods that consider imperfect detection", including mark-recapture and occupancy modelling (Jessop et al. in prep.). Based on 19 years of data in areas of Komodo and Rinca most impacted by tourism and associated infrastructure, as well as on the three small islands within Komodo National Park, the population on these islands is stable or increasing, and density estimates are consistent with those found by Auffenberg in surveys in 1970 (Jessop et al. in prep.).

Extrapolation from around a decade of camera trap site occupancy results on Flores suggests "at least a small chance" that all three subpopulations here are declining; these results contain a high degree of uncertainty (detailed results presented by Jessop et al. in prep.).

There is very little gene flow or dispersal between subpopulations in either Komodo National Park or Flores, and levels of genetic divergence between subpopulations are high (Jessop et al. in prep.). Northern and western subpopulations on Flores are genetically divergent from one another, which modelling by Ciofi et al. (1999) indicated likely represents recent separation likely following habitat loss. Long-distance dispersal events are estimated to occur at a rate of about once a decade (for instance, Padar was not recolonized from a closely-adjacent island for at least three decades after the species was lost here), and the species is" not considered to function as an effective metapopulation" (Jessop et al. in prep.).
documentation.habitats: Individuals have been encountered in a variety of the habitats on Komodo, including monsoon forest, savanna, steppe, mangrove forest and littoral habitats (Auffenberg 1980). It is most abundant in savanna and monsoon forest (Auffenberg 1980). Results of occupancy studies indicate that it prefers forest vegetation in a savanna grassland matrix, and high montane closed montane forest (Jessop et al. in prep.). Juveniles actively search for prey on the ground and in trees (being arboreal for the first year of life - Jessop et al. in prep.), while the terrestrial adults ambush their prey - hatchlings are strictly arboreal (Ciofi in Pianka et al. 2004).  It has a wide prey base, but appears to especially prey on deer, wild pigs and water buffalo (Auffenberg 1980, Koch et al. 2013). In the wild females mature between 6–7 years, and mostly breed annually, however, some also biennial (Jessop et al. in prep.). Males reach maturity at 17 kg (Jessop et al. in prep.). Generation length has been estimated to be 15 years (Jessop et al. in prep.). Up to 30 eggs are laid in nests excavated in the soil (Auffenberg 1980); clutch sizes average at 18 eggs and incubation lasts approx. 220 days at around 28°C (Auliya and Koch 2020, and references therein). Jessop et al. (in prep.) estimated numbers of offspring to successfully hatch as 20 ± 2.5 hatchlings based on a sample of nine fenced nests.
documentation.threats:
The majority of the Komodo Dragon's population lies within Komodo National Park, where it is expected to be "fairly well protected", although small subpopulations on Gili Motan and Padar are likely to be subject to demographic stochasticity die to their low population size and isolation; this considered less of a threat to the Nusa Kode subpopulation, which while small is genetically more diverse (Jessop et al. in prep.). These authors indicate that there is no threat from habitat loss within Komodo National Park, and that the species is at low risk from human activities, illegal harvesting or the impacts of invasive species (cats and goats, which are confined to the main village on both Komodo and Rinca). There is some poaching of the deer on which this species is reliant in Komodo National Park, but this does not presently appear to affect prey populations in this area (Jessop et al. in prep.). Ecotourism appears to have only a "limited" impact, with no evidence of decline over 50 years in areas where this activity is most extensive, including active monitoring over 19 years (Jessop et al. in prep.)

The genetically distinct Flores subpopulation is at ongoing risk, and is likely to be "increasingly affected" by, from habitat loss, which is most widespread on the island's north coast: no more than 10% of the area of occupancy of any Flores subpopulation lies within protected areas, and forest mapping data indicates an ongoing rate of forest loss of about 1% per annum (corresponding to 45% over three generations) (Jessop et al. in prep.). These authors also highlight a major threat from the loss of natural prey to human hunters. The major drivers of habitat loss and fragmentation in this area are subsistence farming and altered fire regimes, and there may also be human-animal conflict over livestock to the north central Flores subpopulation (Koch et al. 2013, Murphy et al. 2002, Jessop et al. in prep.). Cats and dogs are an unknown but possibly significant threat to all Flores subpopulations (Jessop et al. in prep.). Surveys have not recorded the invasive Asian Common Toad (Duttaphrynus melaonistictus), but as this species appears to have adverse impacts on monitor lizards that prey on an invasive population on Sumbawa (S. Reilly pers. comm. 2019) it may represent a potential future threat. There appears to be an illicit trade in live specimens for zoos and the international pet trade (Koch et al. 2013); the source subpopulations are unclear but may be those on Flores where illicit collection is regarded as "medium risk" by Jessop et al. (in prep.).

This species' low dispersal capability and area of occupancy, and the fact that the larger part of the population is restricted to the islands of Komodo National Park, it is expected to be at risk from expected changes in temperature, precipitation and sea level rise (Jessop et al. in prep.). Ecological niche modelling suggests changes in the area of suitable habitat in the period 2010–2040 will decline by 8.4, 30.2% or 71% under three different climate change scenarios. This suggests that a decline in the area of suitable habitat by at least 30% over a 45 year three-generation period is a plausible assumption.
documentation.measures: Jessop et al. (in prep.) recommend that the genetically highly divergent North Flores and Komodo National Park subpopulations be manged as two separate management units. It is listed in CITES Appendix I. This species occurs in the Komodo National Park, and several other protected areas. More research is needed to understand the temperature increase caused by the climate change effects on this species (S. Reilly, D. Iskandar, and E. Arida pers. comm. 2019).
documentation.use_trade: There appears to be illicit trade in this species for the zoo and international pet trade (Koch et al. 2013). In 2011, a seller at the Chatuchat market in Bangkok stated that he could get a half-grown (100 cm total length) animal on request (M. Auliya, pers. comm.). Anecdotal information suggests that juveniles are illegally collected (also see https://www.wfft.org/wildlife-trade/are-komodo-dragons-smuggled-in-to-thailand/). The illegal sale of the species through social media has also been reported.  https://news.mongabay.com/2019/04/indonesia-arrests-7-for-allegedly-selling-komodo-dragons-over-facebook/). In 2014 seizure of Varanus komodoensis were reported, and theft in France (http://www.robindesbois.org/en/a-la-trace-bulletin-dinformation-et-danalyses-sur-le-braconnage-et-la-contrebande/).
documentation.rationale: Listed as Endangered on the basis that this species occurs in eight subpopulations, with a total adult population estimated to contain fewer than 1,400 individuals, no individual subpopulation contains more than 500 individuals, and climate modelling suggests a rate of decline over 40 years from 2010 which may exceed 30% (equating to a decline in excess of 20% across a two-generation period of 30 years), although long-term monitoring on Komodo and Rinca have not yet recorded any declines in occupancy. Additionally, the species has an area of occupancy estimated at 809 km<sup>2</sup>, and certainly below 2,000 km<sup>2</sup>, within which it is considered to occur both as a severely fragmented population (as no more than 34% of the population is in any subpopulation, and rates of genetic exchange are very low) and at eight locations (each representing one subpopulation), and there is a continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat across a third of its range driven by human activities, including agricultural expansion. Although the population as a whole may be broadly stable, the species may be in decline in all areas of Flores where it survives and is under increasing pressure from habitat loss here as well as direct killing or removal of individuals. Efforts to smuggling live animals out of Indonesia, apparently for the pet trade, have been recently recorded.
